One-sentence judgment: calibration technologists and technicians are not about "turning screws and adjusting dials"; they apply knowledge of measurement science, mathematics, physics, chemistry, and electronics to execute or adapt procedures and techniques for calibrating measurement devices, determine whether a measurement standard is suitable for calibrating the device, and perform preventive maintenance and corrective actions on equipment; the output is traceable calibration and test records. O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone Three (medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to below 7.0), marks it Bright Outlook, and gives an interest code of RCI. The core boundary: you may perform calibration, inspection, recording, and equipment maintenance within the authorized scope, but you may not decide on your own whether a reference standard is acceptable, may not replace engineering staff's release conclusions, and may not, without authorization, handle controlled equipment or controlled data or issue conclusions externally.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to measure repeatedly per procedures and record readings, environmental conditions, and gauge status completely; you can accept a mainly indoor, environmentally controlled setting where being exact is extremely important; you are willing to learn gauge use, measurement uncertainty, and sources of error; when data and the shop floor disagree you are willing to recheck before reporting rather than giving a conclusion first; and you accept a daily routine centered on documents, records, and verification.

Conditions for pausing major investment first: you have not yet completed one full closed loop from reading procedures, selecting reference standards, performing calibration, and recording readings through review and reporting; or you are unwilling to check environmental conditions and gauge status per procedures and just want to adjust until it feels right; also, do not treat being able to use a multimeter or having done a course experiment as proof that you can issue calibration conclusions independently.

Education, credentials, and authorization must be checked separately: O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone Three (medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to below 7.0); most positions require training at a vocational school, related on-the-job experience, or an associate degree, and on-the-job training usually takes one to two years. In the United States, job requirements are set by employers; common industry certifications (such as the American Society for Quality's Certified Calibration Technician and Snap-on Industrial's Precision Measuring Instruments Certification) are voluntary certifications, not practice licenses. In mainland China, the Occupational Classification Code of the People's Republic of China (2022 edition) has no one-to-one sub-category matching this entry, and the related duties may fall under metrology, inspection and testing, and instrumentation positions and are carried out under metrology regulations and metrology technical specifications; they must be judged by the actual duties of the position, and it is made clear that the Chinese page language does not constitute a China-equivalent occupation or wage mapping. Credentials, equipment operating authorization, the right to sign calibration conclusions, and controlled-data access rights are four different things and cannot substitute for one another.

In one sentence: this is a role that turns "is the measurement trustworthy" into traceable evidence; the outputs are calibration and test records that follow procedures, deviation and uncertainty notes, equipment maintenance and corrective action records, and a chain traceable to reference standards; it is not the approving role for design or release, nor does it replace the legal requirements of metrology regulations and the final determination of the company's quality system. This page does not publish occupation-level wage figures for mainland China and only registers the scope and gaps with visible markers.

The work of this occupation falls into three categories: first, calibration and testing (determining measurement standards and gauges per procedures, comparing against known standards and performing calibration tests, using precision gauges to check dimensions and clearances, analyzing test data and judging deviations); second, equipment and maintenance (maintaining and repairing measurement equipment, disassembling and reassembling for inspection, visually inspecting for surface defects, ordering replacement parts, taking corrective actions); third, records and standards (writing and submitting calibration reports, planning test sequences per equipment specifications and scientific principles, reading drawings, schematics, and technical specifications, developing new calibration methods, and attending training to update knowledge). All three share the same chain built around procedures, reference standards, and record traceability.
Calibration and testing

Editorial process example: confirm the object, purpose, and method → check the environment and reference standards → record measurements → analyze the relationship and uncertainty; when adjustment or repair is needed, check the conditions separately and recalibrate as required afterwards. In China, calibration determines the relationship between the indicated value of a measuring instrument and the value of the measurement standard, along with the uncertainty; verification has its own legal requirements and conformity conclusion, and calibration does not automatically replace verification, adjustment and repair, or product release. The specific method and conformity judgment are checked separately per the applicable specifications, purpose, and agreement.
Equipment and maintenance

Editorial maintenance interface example: check equipment condition and the applicable safety procedures, and only when actually needed and with the ability and authority, disassemble, clean, repair, reassemble, and verify, with recalibration decided by the method; not every unit sent for calibration must be disassembled, and this grants readers no operating authority.

Editorial handover check: check the method, environment, reference standards, and data, and when an abnormality is found restrict use and assess the impact per the real procedures. Metrological traceability pertains to the measurement result and requires a documented unbroken calibration chain with the uncertainty of each link; a device label or certificate number alone does not guarantee that the result is fit for the intended use.

Calibration technologists and technicians have as their core output procedure-compliant calibration and test records, deviation notes, and a traceable chain; electronics engineers (except computer) are responsible for the design and schemes of circuits and systems, with output mainly design documents and systems; validation engineers are responsible for establishing and maintaining validation plans and compliance evidence, with output mainly validation strategy and documentation systems; mechanical engineers are responsible for the design calculations of mechanical systems and components, with output mainly design drawings and calculation sheets; mechatronics engineers are responsible for the integrated design of electromechanical systems and automation; aerospace engineering and operations technologists provide engineering support and operations data work in the aviation field; electrical and electronic engineering technologists build, test, and repair electrical and electronic systems under the direction of engineers. Similar names or being in the same engineering and testing chain do not mean that design authority, release authority, and the right to sign calibration conclusions are interchangeable.
Core purpose

Calibration uses an appropriate standard and method to determine the value relationship and uncertainty and provides reviewable records; traceability itself does not guarantee that a measurement is suitable for all uses.
Main objects and basis

The objects are measurement devices and instruments, reference standards and reference materials, drawings, schematics, and technical specifications, precision gauges and calibration fixtures, environmental conditions (temperature, humidity, etc.), calibration and test data, and equipment maintenance and replacement parts; the basis is calibration procedures and metrology technical specifications, equipment specifications and scientific principles, the traceability requirements for gauges and reference standards, accuracy and uncertainty requirements, the record and release procedures of the company's quality system, and the access rules for controlled equipment and data.
Core process

Reading procedures and drawings, checking the environment and reference standards, performing calibration and testing, recording readings, analyzing data and judging deviations, adjusting or repairing equipment, disassembly and reassembly, visual inspection, planning test sequences, writing reports, and review and filing.
Main outputs

Calibration and test records that follow procedures, deviation and uncertainty notes, equipment maintenance and corrective action records, status and traceability records for reference standards and gauges, calibration reports, test sequence and process notes, and handover and filing notes.
Accountable party

Editorial responsibility interface example: measurement, reference standard management, design, quality sign-off, and information management may be separated or combined; check against the real position system, and the occupation name does not assign exclusive responsibility.
Authority and approval

Metrology standard assessment, the institution's business scope, personnel competence, and equipment/data authorization are checked separately; Article 6 of the 2025 metrology standard assessment measures read requires equipment certificates for the applicable standard, the environment, and at least 2 personnel with the corresponding competence. The internal highest standards in the six pilot cities have specific exemptions but still require traceability; these exemptions do not apply to uses such as external calibration. Calibration technologists and technicians (O*NET-SOC 17-3028.00) execute or adapt procedures and techniques for calibrating measurement devices, applying knowledge of measurement science, mathematics, physics, chemistry, and electronics, sometimes working under the direction of engineering staff; they determine the suitability of measurement standards for calibrating measurement devices, and perform preventive maintenance on equipment and corrective actions for identified calibration problems. Daily work includes: maintaining or repairing measurement devices and equipment used for calibration testing; using precision gauges to check whether part dimensions or clearances meet specifications; performing calibration tests on mechanical, structural, or electromechanical equipment to determine its performance or reliability; reading drawings, schematics, diagrams, and technical specifications; visually inspecting equipment to find surface defects; calibrating devices by comparing measurements of environmental conditions such as pressure, temperature, and humidity against known standards; disassembling and reassembling equipment for inspection; analyzing test data to identify defects or determine calibration requirements; planning the sequence of calibration tests per equipment specifications and scientific principles; ordering replacement parts for faulty equipment; developing new calibration methods based on measurement science, analysis, or calibration requirements; writing and submitting reports of calibration test results; attending training to learn new tools and methods; and they may also draw designs for tooling, fixtures, and instruments. They carry responsibility for the traceability of measurements and records, the status of gauges and reference standards, and explanation of calibration deviations, but do not replace design release, legal metrology determinations, or the final approval of the company's quality system.

paragraphs: This page compares calibration technologists and technicians with five adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: career direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which direction each preference is better suited to. Adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupation descriptions and do not mean the job titles are interchangeable.

Evidence note: the career direction and core outputs are based on O*NET 17-3028.00 and the official descriptions of the adjacent entries (U.S. scope); equipment and reference standard authorization, the right to sign calibration conclusions, and controlled-data access rights must be verified separately for each company and jurisdiction, and this page does not present any direction as a shortcut for changing careers.

The table below compares the differences in duties and outputs between calibration technologists and technicians and the adjacent directions; the basis for judging is the main outputs, what the work is accountable for, and the required authorization, not how similar the job titles are.

Electronics engineers are responsible for whether a scheme holds up and need design calculations and release judgments; this occupation is responsible for whether measurement results are trustworthy, performing calibration, testing, and recording under established procedures without changing design criteria on their own.

If you would rather do circuit and system design and carry scheme responsibility, look first at the electronics engineer direction; if you would rather do measurement, verification, and recording under procedures, look first at this occupation.
Responsible for the design, development, and scheme validation of circuits and electronic systems, with output mainly design documents and systems.
Electronics Engineers (except Computer)

Validation engineers focus on the compliance of processes and documentation systems and need to design and review validation strategies; this occupation focuses on the measurement trustworthiness of specific equipment, performing calibration and testing under procedures and recording data.

If you would rather design and review validation plans and compliance documents, look first at the validation engineer direction; if you would rather perform calibration, testing, and equipment maintenance on the front line, look first at this occupation.
Establish and maintain validation plans, test strategies, and compliance evidence, with output mainly the validation documentation system.
Validation Engineers

Mechanical engineers face design judgments about loads, materials, and structures, and their responsibility lies in whether the design holds up; this occupation faces gauges, reference standards, and measurement conditions, and its responsibility lies in whether the measurement is trustworthy and traceable.

If you would rather do mechanical design and calculation, look first at the mechanical engineer direction; if you would rather do precision measurement and equipment maintenance, look first at this occupation.
Design mechanical systems and components and carry out calculations and selection, with output mainly design drawings and calculation sheets.
Mechanical Engineers

Mechatronics engineers carry design responsibility for system integration and control logic; this occupation carries responsibility for the accuracy and records of the measurement chain, focusing on reference standards, gauges, and environmental conditions.

If you would rather do mechatronic system integration and control commissioning, look first at the mechatronics engineer direction; if you would rather do precision work in measurement and calibration, look first at this occupation.
Integrate mechanical, electronic, and control elements, and design and commission automated systems, with output mainly integration schemes and commissioning results.
Mechatronics Engineers

Technicians in that direction support engineering and operations in specific industry settings and are bound by industry standards; this occupation provides measurement and calibration services across industries, and is accountable for measurement results and equipment status.

If you would rather do engineering support and operations in a specific industry setting, look first at the aerospace engineering and operations technologist direction; if you would rather do general measurement and calibration, look first at this occupation.
Provide engineering support, data compilation, and operations coordination in the aviation field, with output mainly engineering data and operations records.
Aerospace Engineering and Operations Technologists and Technicians

Electrical and electronic engineering technologists lean toward system build-up and fault repair, with criteria coming from system function; this occupation leans toward the calibration and verification of measurement devices, with criteria coming from reference standards and accuracy requirements.

If you would rather build and repair electrical and electronic systems, look first at the electrical and electronic engineering technologist direction; if you would rather do calibration and verification, look first at this occupation.
Build, test, and repair electrical and electronic systems under the direction of engineers, with output mainly test data and repair records.
Electrical and Electronic Engineering Technologists and Technicians

Conclusion: the choice of direction is based on the main outputs, what the work is accountable for, and the required authorization, not on how similar the names are; once the direction is set, check the target position item by item for the authorized scope of equipment and reference standards, the signing and review process for calibration conclusions, controlled-data requirements, and shifts and site conditions, and keep written confirmation.

paragraphs: Boundary: this section describes occupational risk and responsibility boundaries, not an evaluation of any individual or institution; specific procedures and handling processes are determined by the applicable jurisdiction, metrology technical specifications, and the institution's quality management system.

Editorial risk examples: abnormal or overdue reference standards, environmental exceedance, records that cannot be reviewed, unauthorized data access, unauthorized changes to the method or reference standard, and signing without appropriate authorization. The consequences depend on the measurement purpose and impact assessment, and it cannot be said that all results and reviews must fail. The OOH also notes noisy machinery, toxic materials, and moving heavy equipment, and protection is checked per task.

O*NET provides occupational activities and context; SAMR provides the boundaries of calibration/verification and the assessment of applicable standards; NIST provides traceability and recalibration explanations. entries.answer: Apply knowledge of measurement science, mathematics, physics, chemistry, and electronics to execute or adapt procedures and techniques for calibrating measurement devices; maintain or repair measurement devices used for calibration testing; use precision gauges to check whether part dimensions or clearances meet specifications; perform calibration tests on mechanical, structural, or electromechanical equipment to determine performance or reliability; read drawings, schematics, and technical specifications; visually inspect equipment for surface defects; calibrate devices by comparing measurements of pressure, temperature, humidity, and other conditions against known standards; disassemble and reassemble equipment for inspection; analyze test data to identify defects or determine calibration requirements; plan test sequences per equipment specifications and scientific principles; order replacement parts for faulty equipment; write and submit calibration reports; and attend training to learn new tools and methods.
entries.question: What do calibration technologists and technicians do every day?

entries.answer: The main risks are all measurement results becoming invalid because a reference standard is out of adjustment or overdue, systematic bias from exceeding environmental conditions, conclusions becoming untraceable because data records are incomplete, controlled equipment and data being accessed without authorization, adjusting criteria or swapping reference standards beyond authorization, and personal and equipment injury during disassembly and handling; control depends on periodic traceability of reference standards and gauges, checking environmental conditions, complete raw records, controlled-data management, and clear authorization and escalation procedures.
entries.question: What risks does this job most require you to watch out for in advance?

entries.answer: Fit signals are being able to read procedures and drawings and perform measurements as required, keeping records complete and traceable, and decommissioning and reporting first when a reference standard is overdue or data are abnormal; being able to use a multimeter or having done a course experiment is not enough to prove competence — what matters is whether there is reviewable measurement accuracy, traceability records, and standard operating habits.
entries.question: How do you judge whether this job suits you?

entries.answer: Retrieval of procedures and criteria, organizing measurement data and summarizing deviations, drafting reports, compiling the calibration log and traceability records, and maintenance reminders and replacement part lists can be assisted; reference standard suitability judgments, measurement and deviation conclusions, equipment status confirmation, and controlled-data handling are still checked and owned by the workers.

subject.name: Calibration Technologists and Technicians
subject.summary: This page's entry corresponds to calibration technologists and technicians (O*NET-SOC 17-3028.00): executing or adapting procedures and techniques for calibrating measurement devices, applying knowledge of measurement science, mathematics, physics, chemistry, and electronics, and determining the suitability of measurement standards for calibrating measurement devices — comparison measurement to procedures, checking dimensions and clearances, analyzing deviations, disassembling and maintaining equipment, and writing calibration reports; the work is mainly precision operations and recording under environmentally controlled indoor conditions (indoors environmentally controlled 97, being exact or highly accurate extremely important 89, sitting continuously 58, standing continuously 51), and its responsibility does not equal design release or final approval of external reports.
